Ms. Ikenberry obtained extensive training in paradigmatic techniques with Mrs. Nelson and with her co-edited Psychosexual Imperatives: Their Role in Identity Formation.

Introduction

The hallmark of Marie Coleman Nelson's paradigmatic technique is her ingenious ability to deftly use multiple role models for therapeutic gain. It has not been sufficiently recognized that in adopting such a foundation, paradigmatic therapy affords a radical re-visualization of therapeutic process. Friedman's (1979) paper is a recent exception which deserves careful study.

The material presented here is based on a recent workshop presented by Marie Coleman Nelson and three other contemporary therapists on current approaches to treatment of the borderline patient.* A review of the various clinical presentations given at this workshop disclosed among other things the singularity of Nelson's therapeutic approach.

Case Material

Nelson presented several sessions with a borderline patient, each of which helped to demonstrate the effect of paradigmatic techniques.

Paradigmatic psychotherapy was developed by Marie Coleman Nelson, and her now classic paper “Externalization of the toxic introject” (Coleman, 1956) was the first report of her efforts at devising innovative techniques for treating the narcissistic disorders within the framework of psychoanalysis. In that paper Nelson offered a theory and a developing rationale for paradigmatic interventions to bypass the stalemates that occur in interpretive failures. Paradigmatic technique eschews direct interpretation and provides an optimal approach to the rational and healthy parts of the patient's ego, it offers the most control over the necessary tension for therapeutic interaction and management of the transference. Early on she attempted to adjust theory and therapy to cognitive psychology. With paradigmatic therapy she presents an indirect communication which does not join the patient's defense but bypasses it in a subliminal way, thus eroding the resistance.

The purpose of this paper is to explore what I believe to be some of the powerfully humanistic antecedents of the paradigmatic approach, a factor that is often overlooked when the technique is employed mindlessly or understood in a truncated way by practitioners, without appreciation of the theory on which the technique is based. (The unfamiliar reader is referred to the book Roles and Paradigms in Psychotherapy Nelson et al., 1968.)

Since the work of Abraham and Wilhelm Reich, psychoanalysts have become increasingly interested in the understanding and treatment of character disorder. The effort to conceptualize the nature and pathology of character has been one of the major forces behind the development of psychoanalytic ego psychology. However, most theories of the ego so far formulated consist of a hodge-podge of concepts from the theory of instinctual drives with a rather mysterious, relatively autonomous ego tacked on. Reading Theodore Saretsky's Resolving Treatment Impasses: The Difficult Patient, left me with a strong impression of what's right about

241

psychoanalysis, an impression rendered all the more powerful by simultaneous reading of Janet Malcolm's brilliant study of classical psychoanalysis, in Psychoanalysis: The Impossible Profession.

Saretsky's book is academic and intellectually demanding and is directed to the practicing professional. Malcolm's book, which was originally published in The New Yorker magazine, is meant for the lay reader and consists largely of material gathered during a series of interviews with a practicing New York City analyst. It is a personal and often touching account of the internal and external life of a psychoanalyst.

These, however, are only the surface differences. More important differences are those that represent the heart of the divergencies in thinking of contemporary psychoanalysis.

Disagreements over application of technique or even over the correctness of theory are not new. They are part of the history of Freud's relations with his disciples. Breaches in thinking resulted in the rupture of several long-term and important relations to Freud. Disagreements are hardly less bitter today.

Melanie Klein's interest in the very early years of life marked a departure from Freud's emphasis on the developmentally late oedipal conflict. Her example inspired analysts to take increasing liberties in broadening theory and technique. Saretsky's chapter, “The Imperfect Container,” gives a clear and thoughtful elucidation of the history and implications of these changes. Lang's “bipersonal field” is referred to; Sullivan's construct of participant observer; Searles' provocative idea of the curative process being bi-directional—the patient cures the analyst as well as the analyst curing the patient.

Saretsky observes that: 1) Interpretation, without a prior establishment of trust and feeling, can be experienced by the patient as a “persecutory assault.” 2) The analyst's participation in “shared behavioral experiences” (by which I understand Saretsky to mean the capacity of the analyst to be feeling fully connected to the patient) is a precursor to successful treatment. 3) Treatment impasses can be rooted in unresolved transference/countertransference issues (and here, I believe Saretsky means the emphasis to be on the countertransference).

Marie Nelson

Marie Nelson

P.O. Box 48434
Nairobi, Kenya

Marie Nelson   Has had a long and active career in the psychoanalytic world as clinician, author, editor, teacher, supervisor and lecturer. She is best known for her contributions in paradigmatic psychotherapy and parapsychology. Describing herself as a reformed workaholic, Mrs. Nelson, now residing in Kenya, continues to provide supervision via airmail tapes and to edit the Self-in-Process Series for Human Sciences Press, as well as to engage in writing and research of her own.

Paradigmatic psychotherapy evolved in response to therapeutic needs that cannot be met by standard methods of interpretation. Conceptually, it approaches a theory of treatment which bridges the divide between the latest advance of the classical Freudian school, ego psychology (19), and the work of the object-relations schools of therapy (10, 16).

Certainly the background of a highly authoritarian and paternalistic culture contributed to the historic emergence of Freud's revolutionary theory of psychic organization and function, and it is hardly the exclusive result of scientific progress that psychoanalysts of today turn their sights to the problems associated with narcissism. Contemporary society reinforces addictive, voyeuristic, unstructured and fantasy-laden experience and through increased opportunities for mobility and the impact of the communications media exposes the child from infancy to a bewildering and stimulating array of role enactments and behavioral options (31). In consequence we are obliged to evolve techniques for the treatment of patients (1) whose span of attention is comparatively attenuated because of the kaleidoscopic fragmentation of life experiences, (2) who are conditioned to simultaneously ward off stimuli and to crave stimuli (e.g., the child who cannot do homework unless the radio or TV is on), and (3) who are more provisional and transitory in their conscious identifications and less ready to cathect any particular therapeutic agency or method of treatment.

A middle aged woman consulted the author about her marital situation. The marriage was stable until the husband stopped drinking and began to lose weight. At that point he discovered that other women were attracted to him and he became openly critical of the wife and her treatment of him. The husband agreed to enter therapy with the goal of understanding himself and effecting a resolution of the situation. During the fourth session he began talking about his girl friend. I immediately began thinking about driving from the South Shore to the North Shore, passing the Long Island Expressway, to visit Nelson, who was at that time my supervisor. The patient then told me that he recently felt compelled to get in his car and drive north to the Long Island Expressway to a long-term parking area. Upon doing this he met his girl friend leaving the lot. Neither could explain what had drawn them to this spot. It was not their habit to meet there. I understood my precognitive anticipation of the patient's parking lot communication as well as his paranormal experience of a symbiotic relatedness between us and between the patient and his girlfriend. Knowing the patient's history of alcholism and early abandonment, I formulated an intervention designed to resolve his status quo resistance (complaining about his wife) and activate in the treatment those feelings which the resistance and, earlier, the alcoholism, prevented him from experiencing.

The editor of this series speaks, in the Preface, of the academic fondness for the idea of “the unconscious without Freud.” Transactional Analysis was proposed by its creator, Eric Berne, as “Freud without the unconscious.” London TA specialist Mavis Klein presents a concise and lively exposition in the first British textbook

250

about the theory and therapy of what she calls “the bastard child of psychoanalysis and operant conditioning.”

Berne's frustration with the slowness of psychoanalytic progress led him to question the “rules” that call for passivity in the analyst and individual treatment as a modality. He felt strongly that patients could be helped to feel and act better first and to resolve their underlying conflicts later. To that end, he developed an elaborate and detailed expositive theory of psychoanalytic ego psychology, focused on the conscious elements of personality. From this came the colloquial language of TA and a systemized approach to therapy.

Language in TA is a central issue. The simplicity of the vocabulary communicates quickly and concisely an array of sophisticated perceptions. The intention is to facilitate rapid communication and understanding, and the modality is group therapy. Patients make contracts in ego state language; have constant reference and access to the therapist's notes; are wholly responsible for their own goals and decisions; and are required to engage their whole egos in the process.

There's much more to this book than theoretical exposition and language translation. Klein has put together an easily deciphered textbook of a relatively new psychotherapy, along with transcripts of a diagnostic interview and a group session, with comments and notes. Four case histories are included.

The roots of TA are clearly mainstream Freudian, with admixtures of Adler, Jung, Rank, and, though Berne never seemed aware of it, B.F. Skinner.

Is a new spirit of ecumenicism making itself felt in the land of psychoanalysis? It would be most welcome if it were, surely. These two books seem to provide a bit of evidence for it, to add to such phenomena as the splendid interdisciplinary conferences of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis and for that matter the very existence, not to say burgeoning, of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis itself.

The two volumes, though they differ in focus and emphasis, set about similar tasks: each means to present its intended readership with insight into a variety of therapeutic styles and theories by allowing practitioners to speak for themselves in one way or another. Each manages to do this with impressive fairness while covering a broad spectrum of schools.

“Family psychiatry,” Dr. Howells says in his preface, “is not family therapy, but as one American family therapist put it ‘the field of family therapy is to be considered a branch of the broader discipline of family psychiatry.’” Both are represented in this volume. Family psychiatry, with its fulcrum in the United Kingdom, is broad in scope, and its core idea is that the family is the unit throughout clinical practice—for psychopathology, diagnosis, and treatment. Family therapy, with its fulcrum in the United States, is a narrower approach, but of considerable size, with an emphasis on treatment. This book covers all aspects of family psychiatry—theory, family psychopathology, family diagnosis, family symptomatology, family psychotherapy, and vector therapy. Consists of 36 recent papers from a wide variety of journals in seven countries, in 542 close-set pages, and with indexes.

Introduction

The array of therapeutic techniques available to analysts is so broad as to be downright alarming. Like our experienced patients who are in their second analysis, or who are simultaneously in group, individual, and couples treatment, we have a potpourri of at times interrelated, at times mutually exclusive techniques to draw upon.

This paper will focus on a specific psychotherapeutic technique, called paradigmatic, with a particular type of patient—a borderline man with schizoid, paranoid, depressive and masochistic features— and will present the therapeutic process during three sessions with the patient. Dr. Otto Kernberg's descriptions of the internal phenomenology of the “borderline mind” and the treatment process with such patients is relevant here.

Perhaps the most striking characteristic of the transference manifestations of patients with borderline personality organization is the premature activation in the transference of very early conflict-laden object relationships in the context of ego states that are dissociated from each other. It is as if each of these ego states represents a full-fledged transference paradigm, a highly developed, regressive transference reaction within which a specific internalized object relationship is activated in the transference.

Marie Coleman Nelson (1968) has derived a technique for psychoanalytic therapy based on the enactment of various roles by the therapist which are inherent in an individual's personality. She uses this role-playing technique to resolve resistance and promote maturational growth.

My intention is to recapitulate some of her ideas, connecting them where possible to other aspects of psychoanalytic treatment and to my own experience as a clinician. Included are observations from two week-long seminars taught by Nelson which were sponsored by Heed University.

The paradigmatic approach as developed and explained by Nelson pays particular attention to roles the patient plays and to introjects which are the identifications to objects inherent in those roles. In The Ego and the Id Freud described the ego as a precipitate of abandoned object cathexes. Melanie Klein discusses object relationships in terms of an introjection into the ego from infancy of part objects such as the breast and then whole objects like parental figures. Hanna Segal (1964) in her work on Klein states that “It is by analyzing the ego's relations with objects internal and external and altering the phantasies about these objects, that we can materially affect the ego's more permanent structure.

In her 1958 paper, “The Paranormal Triangle in Analytic Supervision,” Marie Coleman Nelson attempted to make sense of certain data observed during her analyses and in the supervision of trainees by boldly applying the psi hypothesis (Coleman, 1958). This enabled her to take fullest advantage of psychoanalytic hypotheses in patients whose cases were being supervised. In one case she herself was the trainee. Because of psychosomatic developments in an analytic patient, she arranged to be supervised by a male psychiatrist. Immediately following her first control conference, the patient, who had already been in treatment for two years, began his analytic session with the cheerful exclamation, “I can't understand it, but I feel as though I have just acquired a good father!” In a second case, a patient whose analyst was in supervision with Coleman had a dream mirroring a highly specific set of events in Coleman's experience. In a third case, during an interval between a supervisory hour and the next therapeutic session, a patient appeared to act upon Coleman's supervisory recommendations concerning the handling of specific sexual material before the therapist had had an opportunity to engage the patient in exploring this material. In a fourth case, a patient's employer for the first time confronted him about a certain characterological problem just after Coleman had done so, almost as if he had heard what had transpired and had acted upon it.

In a recent essay on mid-twentieth-century man entitled The Quest for Identity, Dr. Allen Wheelis concerns himself with the relevance of psychoanalysis to the malaise of our time. Exploring the implications and consequences of accelerating social change, Wheelis attributes new patterns of personal unrest and uncertainty to the decline of the superego, the diminished unconscious, and the undermining of traditional values and ways of adjusting to life. In contrast to the patient consulting an analyst in Freud's day, the mid-twentieth-century analysand often appears “burdened by a sense of futility and longs for something or someone to give meaning to his life, to tell him who he is, to give him something to live for.”*

As social change of sufficient magnitude requiring adaptive characterological change has occurred, psychoanalysis as a psychotherapy has attempted to become equally adaptive. Innovations in therapy, therefore, have to be viewed as part and parcel of evolving society. For example, Freud's thought was molded by the cultural atmosphere of the period that ended with the First World War.

Yonata Feldman

Yonata Feldman

16 West 10 Street
New York, N.Y. 10011

Yonata Feldman   (1891-1981) was a renowned social worker and psychoanalyst who taught at Smith College, Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, Columbia University, and Western Reserve. She was noted for her work with children and was active in training child workers at the Jewish Board of Guardians and at other agencies, hospitals, and organizations. She was the author of numerous articles on training, supervision and treatment. The paper presented here was her last work before her death.

My long years of observation of mothers and children while working at The Jewish Board of Guardians lead me to the conclusion that there is a definite relationship between the feelings of the mother during pregnancy and the “emotional reactions” and development of the fetus. It seems to me that unwanted fetuses must experience the fear of death and wanted fetuses experience a feeling of pleasure and well-being. Mothers who did not want their pregnancies for one reason or another and tried to harm themselves physically, or did not eat the proper food, often bore infants who were characteristically colicky, cranky, cried, and had feeding difficulties. Consequently, the mother and child often became engaged in an endless battle of hate and neglect. It is well known that many women who did not want their children killed their infants, flushed them down toilets, or abandoned them.

It is quite obvious to me that those infants who by chance survived and grew up incorporated a destructive self-hate that prevented a successful adult adjustment. It seemed that no matter what therapeutic help was received in later life, unless this intrauteral fear of death was worked through in the transference situation, there was little hope for them.

*Dedicated to Dr. and Mrs. Dominick Riccio without whose help this paper could not have been written183

The aim of modern psychoanalysis is not to provide a corrective emotional experience, to offer insight, to reconstruct the past, to afford catharsis, or to repair the ego, although all these things may occur. The purpose of treatment is for the analyst to resolve the patient's resistance to feeling, thinking and remembering everything—and putting it all into words.

What Spotnitz and his colleagues call Modern Psychoanalysis is an expansion of classical technique that evolved in response to the impasses that tended to develop in the treatment of preoedipal conditions. Finding that interpretation was not usually effective with such patients, modern psychoanalysts extended the range of their interventions. They regard a most significant contribution to technique as being the emphasis on the role of emotional communication, especially in the analyst's interventions.

Freud's writings have provided the source for two lines of development of psychoanalytic technique. In one, described by Sterba in 1934, the analyst helps the patient to dissociate the reasonable part of the ego from the drives and defenses that arise in the transference. The analyst and patient, together examine the events of the transference in a state of affective detachment.

One of the principal ways that patients and analysts have of communicating with each other is by means of questions. It is also a basic way that people have of learning about each other and becoming comfortable with one another. Especially in the beginning phases of treatment, questions are critical to laying the ground work for a productive and smooth-flowing therapeutic relationship. In the initial interview the analyst tends to direct many questions to the patient in order to understand the presenting problem, gain some diagnostic perspective, and get some personal background. In most instances patients are cooperative in yielding abundant information about themselves and their situations. Things often begin to get more difficult after the initial introduction has been accomplished and the roles get reversed: the analyst settles down to listen rather than ask questions, and the patients are expected to spontaneously produce verbal communications about themselves. Although most people proceed to do this, quite a few find it difficult or are unable to adhere to the preferred analytic task of expressing their thoughts and feelings. These people often compulsively either ask many questions about the analyst or the treatment or continually seek advice in the form of questions. The method or process the analyst uses in responding to these questions can in itself constitute a body of technique.

In thinking about severe emotional illness, modern analysts have come to view the solutions patients use to deal with their emotional conflicts to be variations on patterns of turning destructive impulses inward. It helps if we view these solutions as organized mental activity in which the flow of energy can be understood as a method for mastering tension. Using object language to think about the regressed patient is usually an error. Pleasure-pain, tension reduction, overstimulation are terms which better fit the longings and rage with which the narcissistic patient is struggling. Drive theory provides us with the picture of conflict as an insufficient quantity of libido in the system to cope with the amount of tension.

It is clear in a reading of the psychoanalytic literature that despite our experience of treatment with the regressed aspects of a patient, thinking in drive theory terms is difficult for the analyst. When writing, we tend to convert phenomenological experience into self-object representations. When the feeling in the room with a patient is of vast spaces, we describe it as aloneness or emptiness. This is understandable since no psyche stood still at the periods we are recapturing. Layers of pre-object and object experience are added to the surviving psyche.

I. Introduction

Psychoanalysis originated, as all students know, in the treatment of hysterical patients by catharsis. Hysteria had previously been considered due to some sort of constitutional deficiency. Breuer and Freud maintained that certain events had occurred in the life of the hysteric, which later turned out to have had a traumatic significance. The patients in their state of hysteria could not recall these events, but if induced by hypnosis or other means to remember, the patient did recall the event and then abreacted the repressed emotions. This sequence was most clearly evident in the case of Anna O., who discovered the cathartic method practically by herself; i.e. she, on her own initiative, “talked out” the events that gave rise to her hysterical symptoms. Anna O. manifested literally no resistance, and it is doubtful if any patient since that time has been as cooperative in giving forth the historical information relevant to his neurosis.

When Freud began to treat hysterical patients he followed Breuer's lead and searched actively for traumatic incidents; however, the harder he searched the more reluctant the patients became.

He is a founder, Dean of Students, and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies; a founder and training and control analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis. In an earlier paper (Margolis, 1979), the writer offered some preliminary observations on the origins, development and implications for therapy of the narcissistic transference. The present article explores additional aspects of the concept, with the aim of establishing more fully its theoretical and clinical scope.

What is Narcissistic Transference?

Briefly, narcissistic transference is a special form of transference established by the narcissistic patient in the course of analytic therapy. Its characteristics are determined by such factors as the stage of early development at which the patient is fixated, the level of ego formation associated with that stage, and the nature of the experiences that the patient underwent at the time. The narcissistic patient is fixated at some point or points in approximately the first two years of life. In Mahler's (1968, 1975) widely accepted schema of psychological growth, this crucial period covers the first thirty months of life and embraces the developmental stages of normal autism, symbiosis and separation-individuation. Ego formation is conceived as proceeding from one stage to the next. Normal autism is an undifferentiated, objectless state.

It is a great pleasure to present the O. Arnold Bernstein

Arnold Bernstein

Arnold Bernstein  

On May 16, 1980, The Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies presented a program entitled A Dialogue with Marie Coleman Nelson: Her Theories and Techniques in Paradigmatic Therapy. To continue its recognition of the significance of her work, the Journal presents here a tribute in the form of this issue dedicated to her.

Paradigmatic psychotherapy provides a link between ego psychology, object relations theory, and the role concepts of sociologists George Herbert Mead, Charles Cooley, and Benjamin Nelson. It evolved in response to therapeutic needs that could not be met by standard methods of interpretation.

The term “paradigm” implies essentially a “setting forth by example.” Paradigmatic techniques involve the intentional and systematic setting forth of examples by the analyst to assist the patient toward emotional understanding of his intrapsychic processes and his relationships with others. Clinically, paradigmatic therapy utilizes many interventions familiar to modern analysts, as well as role enactment, fantasy participation, and other procedures to facilitate the achievement of insight. The procedures of this psychotherapy are especially effective with characterological and ego syntonic resistances, and Marie Coleman Nelson was a shaper of much of the theory and techniques of paradigmatic psychotherapy.

Introduction

The last fifteen years have seen vastly expanded efforts by women to assert identity as complete and separate individuals. Some women are able to take advantage of the greater opportunities becoming available, while others remain immobilized by feelings of despair, inadequacy, or indiscriminate rage against the world (Symonds, 1974). Feminists have increasingly questioned the ability of social institutions to relate to these difficulties. Within this context, psychoanalysis has come under strong attack in the popular media and the mental health profession. Many critics feel that difficult questions remain unanswered: Is psychoanalysis an outmoded process, unable to respond to the views and goals of contemporary women? Is the theoretical base of psychoanalysis essentially antifemale, working against women's drive for growth and self-realization?

Faced with such challenges to psychoanalysis, the author, as a woman and a modern psychoanalyst, felt the need to respond. Theoretically and in practice, does modern psychoanalysis offer something of particular value to women? Does modern psychoanalysis differ in ways significant to feminists from classical psychoanalysis as depicted in the feminist literature?

Breaking the Frame

Paradigmatic interventions, by modeling aspects of the patient's implicit assumptions, may help the subject get outside himself and the narrow world he is addicted to. They can dramatize in emotionally meaningful ways unconscious imperatives the patient lives or fails to live by. This might take the form of gross caricature on occasion, but, I believe, is most effective when subtly varied, sensitive to modulations of the subject's quality of awareness. These responses, at their best, often are ambiguously overdetermined, “a sort of cryptogram, an encoded message which touches upon but does not make manifest the meaning of the patient's productions.” (M. C. Nelson, 1966, p. 188). From Don Juan's perspective, “the worst thing one can do is confront human beings bluntly.” (Castaneda, 1973b, p. 10; quoted by M. C. Nelson, 1976, p. 351). Such a tactic is easily assimilable by the subject's defenses. One would need to generate situations that stimulate the subject's reach and lead him toward the gap that makes approach possible (Eigen, 1973, 1977; Nelson et al., 1968).

A more general principle that paradigmatic therapy makes its own particular use of involves the art of shifting “sets” or frames of reference. A frame of reference is a system of relations that forms a context for understanding and interpreting reality.

An Interview with Yonata Feldman

Dorothy Gloster C.S.W.

Dorothy Gloster

31 Washington Square West
New York, N.Y. 10011

Dorothy Gloster   Psychothereapist in private practice in New York City. She formerly served on the faculty of the College of Mount St. Vincent and is currently working on an industrial psychology research project investigating the use of group psychotherapy in work settings.

By age 89, Mrs. Yonata Feldman had suffered many years of serious illness; and travel to the various institutions where she taught had become impossible. Her work of treating patients and training professionals in the treatment of emotional problems went on, however. It merely moved to her living room.

Students in analytic training, and supervisors and faculty in the various schools of social work where she served as a faculty member were happy for the privilege of continuing to study with her and made the weekly trip to her home, sat close together around an aluminum folding table, and tried to talk loudly enough to be heard by her. “You know,” she would say, “I'm a little hard of hearing, but once I do hear, I never forget a case.” And just for proof, she would inquire about one of our cases she had supervised years before, remembering it in detail.

As we grew older together and wiser with her, she always seemed to grow younger with us. She continued to astound us with her insight, her willingness to annex new information to an already prodigious store, and to let reign with her dry and ready wit. As her illness progressed and hospital stays became more frequent and longer, she reluctantly and apologetically gave up her regular classes, but granted special appointments when she was able.

Dorothy Bloch

Dorothy Bloch  

Prisoners of Childhood deals with the crippling influence of traumatic early childhood experience and the tenacity of its hold on adults. It is mainly concerned with the “narcissistically cathected” children of narcissistic mothers who use their children to satisfy their neglected narcissistic needs.

Miller is concerned with a special category of children, the gifted, who, in addition, were either only children or first-born. She also deals with a special category of mother, with those having a narcissistic disturbance, who “were extremely insecure and often suffered from depression.” She stresses the serious consequences to the child of an adaptation that is geared to the mother's narcissistic needs, of “the impossibility of experiencing certain feelings of his own (such as jealousy, envy, anger, loneliness, impotence, anxiety).” Although she briefly analyzes the literary output of renowned artists that confirm her observations of patients she has either treated herself or whose treatment she has supervised, her discussion does not distinguish those patients from the general category of patients who “have all developed the art of not experiencing feelings.”

Her emphasis on the importance of allowing children to have and to express their own feelings and on the traumatic effects of repression is the important message of her book.
